items.stem: Which of the following best describes "species diversity"?
options: The range of different habitats in an ecosystem or biome
An event in which at least 75% of species are lost in a geologically short period
The variety of species per unit area, including both the number of species present (richness) and their relative abundance (evenness)
A region with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species that has lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation
items.answer: The variety of species per unit area, including both the number of species present (richness) and their relative abundance (evenness)
items.markingKey: C. "species diversity" is the variety of species per unit area, including both the number of species present (richness) and their relative abundance (evenness).

items.stem: Explain why a community with high evenness is considered more diverse than one dominated by one species.
items.answer: Diversity includes how individuals are distributed among species; if one species dominates, the chance that two random individuals are different species is low, so effective diversity is lower even if richness is the same.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Diversity includes how individuals are distributed among species; if one species dominates, the chance that two random individuals are different species is low, so effective diversity is lower even if richness is the same. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline why genetic diversity is important for the survival of a species.
items.answer: Variation allows some individuals to survive new diseases, predators or climate change, so the population can adapt by natural selection; low diversity increases inbreeding depression and extinction risk (e.g. cheetahs).
items.markingKey: Variation allows some individuals to survive new diseases, predators or climate change, so the population can adapt by natural selection; low diversity increases inbreeding depression and extinction risk (e.g. cheetahs). [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Field data, two grasslands (individuals per species): Meadow A - 10, 10, 10, 10, 10; Meadow B - 46, 1, 1, 1, 1.

Calculate Simpson's reciprocal index for both meadows using D = N(N−1)/Σn(n−1).
items.markingKey: A: N = 50, Σn(n−1) = 5 × 90 = 450, D = 2,450/450 ≈ 5.44; B: Σn(n−1) = 46×45 = 2,070, D = 2,450/2,070 ≈ 1.18. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: A student claims: "Biodiversity simply means the number of species in an area." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and habitat (ecosystem) diversity, and species diversity includes evenness as well as richness.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and habitat (ecosystem) diversity, and species diversity includes evenness as well as richness. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that diversity indices are the best way to measure the health of an ecosystem.
items.answer: Indices are useful indicators but must be combined with indicator species, ecosystem function and conservation status data.
items.markingKey: For: quantitative and comparable over time. Against: do not identify which species (invasives, rare species). [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: Why is genetic diversity important for crop species?
options: It provides traits for breeding resistance to disease, pests and drought
It has no practical importance
It increases fertiliser use
It makes all plants identical
items.answer: It provides traits for breeding resistance to disease, pests and drought
items.markingKey: A. Seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault store it.

items.stem: Explain why the total number of species on Earth is uncertain.
items.answer: Many groups (insects, fungi, nematodes, microbes) are poorly studied; many habitats (deep sea, canopy, soils) are under-sampled; taxonomy is slow; cryptic species are revealed only by DNA analysis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many groups (insects, fungi, nematodes, microbes) are poorly studied; many habitats (deep sea, canopy, soils) are under-sampled; taxonomy is slow; cryptic species are revealed only by DNA analysis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between genetic diversity and species diversity.
items.answer: Species diversity is the variety and relative abundance of species in an area; genetic diversity is the variety of genes and alleles within a population or species.
items.markingKey: Species diversity is the variety and relative abundance of species in an area; genetic diversity is the variety of genes and alleles within a population or species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, Norway shows ex situ conservation of genetic diversity.
items.answer: Opened in 2008 in permafrost rock, it holds over 1.2 million seed samples from almost every country. It backs up crop genetic diversity so lost varieties can be restored, e.g. Syrian ICARDA withdrawals in 2015.
items.markingKey: Context (Opened in 2008 in permafrost rock, it holds over 1.2 million seed samples from almost every country.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It backs up crop genetic diversity so lost varieties can be restored, e.g. Syrian ICARDA withdrawals in 2015. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ex situ conservation of genetic diversity.

items.stem: Outline three reasons why biodiversity should be conserved.
items.answer: Ecological (stability, ecosystem services such as pollination); economic (food, medicines - about half of modern drugs derive from natural compounds; tourism); aesthetic, cultural and ethical (intrinsic value).
items.markingKey: Ecological (stability, ecosystem services such as pollination); economic (food, medicines - about half of modern drugs derive from natural compounds; tourism); aesthetic, cultural and ethical (intrinsic value).

items.stem:
Case study extract - the Irish potato famine (1845-1852): About 1 million people died and 1 million emigrated after potato blight destroyed crops of the genetically uniform Lumper potato.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates the importance of genetic diversity.
items.answer: Low genetic diversity meant almost no plants were resistant, so the pathogen spread through the whole crop.
items.markingKey: Low genetic diversity meant almost no plants were resistant, so the pathogen spread through the whole crop. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to the importance of genetic diversity, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: Distinguish between sympatric speciation and allopatric speciation.
items.answer: Allopatric speciation follows geographical separation of populations; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area through reproductive isolation such as polyploidy or different breeding times.

items.stem: "Mass extinctions have always been caused by asteroids." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most were linked to massive volcanism, climate change, ocean anoxia and acidification; only the end-Cretaceous is strongly linked to an impact.
items.markingKey: Most were linked to massive volcanism, climate change, ocean anoxia and acidification; only the end-Cretaceous is strongly linked to an impact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: About 167 species of freshwater fish (out of roughly 18,000 described species) are documented to have gone extinct in the last 120 years. (a) Calculate the extinction rate in extinctions per million species-years (E/MSY). (b) The background rate is often estimated at about 0.1 E/MSY. Calculate how many times faster than background the observed rate is. (c) Explain why this is likely to be an underestimate.
items.answer: (a) 167 / (18,000 × 120) × 10⁶ = 77.3 E/MSY (b) ≈ 773 times background (c) many species go extinct before they are described; extinctions are only confirmed after long searches; "living dead" (committed) extinctions from habitat loss have not yet happened; some groups are poorly studied.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 extinctions ÷ (species × years) × 10⁶, A1 77.3. (b) A1 ×773. (c) R1 R1 valid reasons / link to mass extinction (≥ 75% of species lost in a geologically short time).

Resource booklet, data extract on the cichlid fish of Lake Malawi: "Over 500-800 species evolved within the lake in less than a few million years."

Using evidence from the extract, analyse what it shows about sympatric and allopatric speciation.
items.answer: Specialisation of jaws and diets plus mate choice by colour created reproductive isolation within one lake.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "The current biodiversity crisis should be considered a sixth mass extinction."
items.answer: We are not yet in a mass extinction by the 75% definition, but current trends could produce one within centuries, which justifies urgent action.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "natural selection".
items.answer: The process by which individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations

items.stem: Outline how geographical isolation can lead to speciation.
items.answer: A barrier (mountain range, sea, river) splits a population; gene flow stops; different selection pressures, mutation and genetic drift cause divergence; eventually the populations can no longer interbreed - reproductive isolation.
items.markingKey: A barrier (mountain range, sea, river) splits a population; gene flow stops; different selection pressures, mutation and genetic drift cause divergence; eventually the populations can no longer interbreed - reproductive isolation. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Using the peppered moth in industrial England as an example, explain natural selection.
items.answer: The dark (carbonaria) form rose to over 90% in Manchester by about 1895 as soot darkened trees, then declined after clean air laws. Predation by birds favoured the better-camouflaged form, changing allele frequencies in response to environmental change.

items.stem: Why does Madagascar have very high endemism (e.g. all lemurs)?

It has been isolated from Africa for about 160 million years and from India for about 88 million years
It has no predators
It was recently formed by volcanoes

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (the peppered moth in industrial England): The dark (carbonaria) form rose to over 90% in Manchester by about 1895 as soot darkened trees, then declined after clean air laws.

Explain what this information reveals about natural selection.
items.answer: Predation by birds favoured the better-camouflaged form, changing allele frequencies in response to environmental change.
items.markingKey: Predation by birds favoured the better-camouflaged form, changing allele frequencies in response to environmental change. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to natural selection, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem:
Resource booklet, data extract on the Sundaland hotspot (Borneo, Sumatra, Java): "Land bridges during glacial periods connected the islands; today it holds about 15,000 endemic plants but has lost over 90% of lowland forest in parts."

Using evidence from the extract, analyse what it shows about plate tectonics, sea-level change and hotspots.
items.answer: Changing connections promoted both dispersal and isolation, producing high endemism now threatened by oil-palm expansion.
items.markingKey: Evidence quoted from the extract with figures/units [1]; Changing connections promoted both dispersal and isolation, producing high endemism now threatened by oil-palm expansion. [1] per valid linked point up to [3].

items.stem: "Isolation is the most important factor in producing high biodiversity." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: Isolation is key for endemism, but overall richness depends on climate, productivity, habitat diversity and time.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: islands and continents show high endemism (Madagascar, Galápagos); allopatric speciation. Arguments challenging it: climate and productivity explain tropical diversity; habitat heterogeneity and time are also important. A supported conclusion might be: Isolation is key for endemism, but overall richness depends on climate, productivity, habitat diversity and time. items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that genetic diversity is more important to conserve than species diversity.
items.answer: All levels are interdependent; genetic diversity is essential for long-term resilience, but it is conserved mainly by protecting species and habitats.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: allows adaptation to climate change and disease; crop genetic diversity underpins food security. Limitations / counter-points: species diversity maintains ecosystem function; genetic diversity cannot be conserved without species and habitats. Conclusion: All levels are interdependent; genetic diversity is essential for long-term resilience, but it is conserved mainly by protecting species and habitats. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the current biodiversity crisis should be considered a sixth mass extinction. [9]
items.answer: We are not yet in a mass extinction by the 75% definition, but current trends could produce one within centuries, which justifies urgent action.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: extinction rates 10-100+ times background; 1 million species threatened (IPBES); rapid, global, human-driven. Arguments challenging it: documented extinctions are still far below 75% of species; data are incomplete and biased; losses are reversible if action is taken. A supported conclusion might be: We are not yet in a mass extinction by the 75% definition, but current trends could produce one within centuries, which justifies urgent action. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "genetic diversity".
items.answer: The range of genetic material present in a population or species
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the range of genetic material present in a population or species. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "allopatric speciation"?
options: Speciation that occurs when populations are geographically isolated and evolve separately
The variety of species per unit area, including both the number of species present (richness) and their relative abundance (evenness)
A region with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species that has lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation
The formation of new and distinct species through evolution
items.answer: Speciation that occurs when populations are geographically isolated and evolve separately
items.markingKey: A. "allopatric speciation" is speciation that occurs when populations are geographically isolated and evolve separately.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "land bridge"?
options: The range of different habitats in an ecosystem or biome
A region with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species that has lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation
The rapid evolution of many species from a common ancestor to fill different niches
A strip of land connecting two landmasses that allows the movement of species, e.g. the Isthmus of Panama or Beringia
items.answer: A strip of land connecting two landmasses that allows the movement of species, e.g. the Isthmus of Panama or Beringia
items.markingKey: D. "land bridge" is a strip of land connecting two landmasses that allows the movement of species, e.g. the Isthmus of Panama or Beringia.

items.stem: "Biodiversity simply means the number of species in an area." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and habitat (ecosystem) diversity, and species diversity includes evenness as well as richness.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and habitat (ecosystem) diversity, and species diversity includes evenness as well as richness. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between background extinction and mass extinction.
items.answer: Background extinction is the normal, low rate of species loss (about 0.1-1 E/MSY); a mass extinction is a geologically rapid loss of at least 75% of species.
items.markingKey: Background extinction is the normal, low rate of species loss (about 0.1-1 E/MSY); a mass extinction is a geologically rapid loss of at least 75% of species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: State two differences between a biodiversity hotspot and a high-biodiversity wilderness area.
items.answer: A hotspot combines high endemism with heavy habitat loss (≥ 70%); a high-biodiversity wilderness area (e.g. the Amazon, Congo) is species-rich but still largely intact.
items.markingKey: A hotspot combines high endemism with heavy habitat loss (≥ 70%); a high-biodiversity wilderness area (e.g. the Amazon, Congo) is species-rich but still largely intact. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: A student claims: "A monoculture plantation with many trees has high biodiversity." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A monoculture has very low species and genetic diversity regardless of how many individuals it has.
items.markingKey: A monoculture has very low species and genetic diversity regardless of how many individuals it has. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why biodiversity hotspots are a priority for conservation.
items.answer: They contain a very high proportion of endemic species in a small area (about half of plant species on 2.5% of land) and are highly threatened (≥70% habitat lost), so conservation here prevents many extinctions per dollar spent.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They contain a very high proportion of endemic species in a small area (about half of plant species on 2.5% of land) and are highly threatened (≥70% habitat lost), so conservation here prevents many extinctions per dollar spent. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Suggest why the cheetah is vulnerable to extinction even in protected areas.
items.answer: A population bottleneck about 10,000 years ago left very low genetic diversity, causing reduced sperm quality, high cub mortality and vulnerability to disease.
items.markingKey: A population bottleneck about 10,000 years ago left very low genetic diversity, causing reduced sperm quality, high cub mortality and vulnerability to disease.

items.stem: In 1977 a drought on Daphne Major (Galápagos) killed many medium ground finches. Survivors had deeper beaks. Explain this observation.
items.answer: Drought reduced small soft seeds; only large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them and survived; beak depth is heritable, so the next generation had deeper beaks (natural selection - Grant and Grant).
items.markingKey: Drought reduced small soft seeds; only large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them and survived; beak depth is heritable, so the next generation had deeper beaks (natural selection - Grant and Grant).

items.stem:
Resource booklet, data extract on the Great American Biotic Interchange: "The Isthmus of Panama formed about 2.7-3 million years ago, allowing armadillos and opossums to move north and big cats, deer and camelids to move south."

Using evidence from the extract, analyse what it shows about land bridges and species distribution.
items.answer: Connection of landmasses mixed faunas, causing competition and extinctions of many South American mammals.

items.markingKey: M1 N = 95 and Σn(n−1) = 1924; A1 D = 4.64. A1 correct rounding/working shown.

items.stem: Briefly describe Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands and explain what it reveals about adaptive radiation and speciation.
items.answer: About 15-18 species evolved from a single ancestral species that arrived from South America about 2-3 million years ago. Isolation on different islands and different food sources selected different beak shapes, producing species that no longer interbreed.
items.markingKey: Context (About 15-18 species evolved from a single ancestral species that arrived from South America about 2-3 million years ago.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that natural selection will allow most species to adapt to rapid climate change.
items.answer: Some species will adapt, but most long-lived species cannot evolve fast enough, so conservation is needed.
items.markingKey: For: short-generation species can evolve quickly (insects, microbes). Against: many large species reproduce slowly. items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Concentrating conservation funding on biodiversity hotspots is the best strategy for protecting global biodiversity."
items.answer: Hotspots are an efficient priority-setting tool but should be combined with protection of wilderness areas, marine systems and community-based conservation.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: protects many endemic species cheaply; focuses on urgent threats. Limitations / counter-points: neglects intact wilderness and oceans; ignores ecosystem services and genetic diversity; may displace local communities. Conclusion: Hotspots are an efficient priority-setting tool but should be combined with protection of wilderness areas, marine systems and community-based conservation. items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that diversity indices are the best way to measure the health of an ecosystem.
items.answer: Indices are useful indicators but must be combined with indicator species, ecosystem function and conservation status data.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: quantitative and comparable over time; include richness and evenness. Limitations / counter-points: do not identify which species (invasives, rare species); depend on sampling effort; ignore genetic and ecosystem diversity. Conclusion: Indices are useful indicators but must be combined with indicator species, ecosystem function and conservation status data.
